candidates.statement: Drug products (e.g., enzyme replacement therapy, enzyme substitution therapy) should be 86 studied in conjunction with dietary management for conditions that use dietary management as 87 part of clinical care. Clinical trials for these drugs typically include measurements of metabolite 88 concentrations (primarily in serum and urine) as endpoints, which are the same assessments used 89 to inform dietary changes and to determine whether dietary management has been optimized. 90 Consequently, dietary changes during these trials can affect efficacy results and pose significant 91 interpretability challenges, particularly when the clinical trial does not anticipate or appropriately 92 account for the confounding effect of diet in the design and analyses of trial results. This 93 confounding can add to the existing challenges in designing and conducting successful clinical 94 trials in rare diseases, such as the limited availability of patients (thus, the small size of clinical 95 trials), the heterogeneity of clinical phenotypes, the challenges with selecting appropriate 96 efficacy endpoints, and the lack of precision of dietary assessments. Inadequate dietary 97 management or insufficient documentation of dietary changes during a trial can make 98 interpretation of trial results particularly difficult when the treatment effect of the new drug 99 product is not large. 100
candidates.context: The goal of dietary modification is to improve or restore biochemical and physiologic 82 homeostasis by restricting the dietary precursors that generate intermediary products of 83 metabolism that may accumulate and lead to toxicity in specific diseases. 84

candidates.statement: Sponsors should consider the following recommendations for optimizing, standardizing, and 107 maintaining the diets of patients before they enter clinical trials: 108
candidates.context: A. Optimizing, Standardizing, and Maintaining Diet Stability in Clinical Trials 105 • When optimizing a patient’s dietary management before trial entry, sponsors should take 110 into account the specific condition that is being treated; the severity of each patient’s 111 metabolic defect; the patient’s age, growth, and general health status; the duration needed 112 to assess whether the patient’s dietary management is appropriate and optimized for the 113 patient’s individual medical needs; and the complexity of, and the patient’s/family’s 114 ability to understand and comply with, the prescribed diet. 115

candidates.statement: Patients with inborn errors of metabolism often require increased caloric intake for procedures or 159 assessments requiring sedation that can include dental care, adenoidectomy or gastrostomy tube 160 placement, in addition to intercurrent illnesses that may precipitate a change in metabolic status 161 (e.g., metabolic decompensation with need for dietary and/or pharmacologic changes). Ideally, 162 sponsors should anticipate and address elective surgeries and procedures before enrolling 163 patients in clinical trials. However, protocols also should specify a standardized approach to 164 dietary management for unanticipated intercurrent procedures, illnesses, and metabolic events 165 that may occur during the trial. Adherence to this approach should be documented 166 systematically and addressed in the statistical analysis plan, including how these intercurrent 167 events will impact the efficacy and safety assessments and clinical interpretation of data. 168

candidates.statement: Although assessments of dietary intake have been used to document dietary practices and to 229 verify the patient’s diet adherence, available tools that measure dietary components have 230 limitations. Sponsors should consider the following: 231
candidates.context: D. Challenges and Limitations of Diet Assessments 227 • Dietary questionnaires use crude measures of portion size, frequency of consumption, 233 and broad food groupings and are only a general estimate of dietary intake. Thus, day-to- 234 day and week-to-week variation in diets could lead to a range of estimates of long-term 235 dietary intake. 5

candidates.statement: • Food diaries (e.g., 3-day diet) are commonly used in the clinical management of patients 238 with inborn errors of metabolism. The inherent variability of patient/family recall in a 239 food diary may introduce imprecision into a clinical trial and should be avoided. Using 240 standardized dietary forms (written or electronic) designed or vetted by metabolic 241 dietitians and physicians can greatly facilitate dietary documentation in a clinical trial and 242 is strongly encouraged. 243
